terms.meaning: The changing shapes of the bright part of the Moon as seen from the Earth.
The time when the bright part grows, from new Moon to full Moon (Shukla Paksha).
The time when the bright part shrinks, from full Moon to new Moon (Krishna Paksha).
An extra month added in a luni-solar calendar to keep it in step with the seasons.
A human-made object launched from the Earth to orbit it.
Old satellites and rocket pieces left in orbit, which can hit working spacecraft.

items.name: Cycle of phases
items.formula: About 29.5 days from one full Moon to the next.
items.example: Two such cycles take about 59 days.

items.name: Why phases happen
items.formula: We see different amounts of the Moon’s sunlit half as it goes around the Earth.
items.example: At new Moon the sunlit half faces away from us.

items.name: Moonrise each day
items.formula: The Moon rises about 50 minutes later each day.
items.example: Tides also come about 50 minutes later each day.

items.name: Why eclipses are not monthly
items.formula: The Moon’s orbit is slightly tilted.
items.example: Usually the Moon’s shadow misses the Earth at new Moon.

items.name: Lunar calendar
items.formula: 12 lunar months = 354 days, so about 11 days shorter than a solar year.
items.example: 12 × 29.5 = 354, and 365 − 354 = 11. Seasons drift through its months.

items.name: Solar calendar
items.formula: Follows the seasons, with a year of 365 days. February gets an extra day every 4 years.
items.example: This makes up for the extra quarter of a day each year: 4 × 1/4 = 1.

items.name: Century leap years
items.formula: A century year is a leap year only if it divides exactly by 400.
items.example: 2000 was a leap year, but 1900 was not.

items.name: Luni-solar calendar
items.formula: Counts months by the Moon, and adds an extra month every 2 to 3 years.

items.name: Indian National Calendar
items.formula: A solar calendar adopted in 1956, starting with Chaitra on 22 March (21 March in a leap year).
items.example: Meghnad Saha chaired the committee behind it.

items.name: Tropical and sidereal year
items.formula: Tropical: spring equinox to spring equinox. Sidereal: back to the same place among the stars, about 20 minutes longer.
items.example: The Gregorian calendar follows the tropical year.

items.name: Festivals set by the Moon
items.formula: Their dates shift in the Gregorian calendar.
items.example: Diwali is on the Amavasya of Kartika, and Holi on the Purnima of Phalguna.

items.name: Festivals set by the Sun
items.example: Makar Sankranti and Pongal come on almost the same date every year.

items.name: India’s space missions
items.formula: Chandrayaan: the Moon. Aditya-L1: the Sun. Mangalyaan: Mars. AstroSat: stars and galaxies.

items.name: Uses of satellites
items.formula: Communication, navigation, weather and watching the Earth.
items.example: Weather satellites help us to track cyclones.

mistakes.text: The Moon’s phases are not caused by the Earth’s shadow. The Earth’s shadow on the Moon is a lunar eclipse.
The Sun always lights half of the Moon. Only the part of it that we can see changes.
Not every year divisible by 4 is a leap year: 1900 divides by 4 but was not one.
